entities.name: Temple of Aphrodite at Acrocorinth
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of Aphrodite at Acrocorinth — positioned dramatically atop the Acrocorinth (the massive 575-meter rock citadel above ancient Corinth in the Peloponnese) — was one of the most famous and controversial sacred sites in the ancient Mediterranean world. Ancient sources, particularly Strabo, describe the temple as housing up to 1,000 sacred prostitutes (hierodouloi) who served the goddess of love through sacred sexual service — a claim that, while probably exaggerated, made Acrocorinth synonymous in ancient literary culture with the extremes of Aphrodite's worship and the wealth and sensuality of Corinthian commercial life.

Corinth's position at the isthmus connecting mainland Greece with the Peloponnese — through which all land traffic and much ship cargo was portaged — made it one of antiquity's wealthiest cities. The city's reputation for luxury, prostitution, and Aphrodite's extravagant worship was proverbial: 'not everyone can afford the journey to Corinth' (Greek proverb about its expensive pleasures). The Acrocorinth sanctuary, whether or not Strabo's numbers are accurate, was certainly an important Aphrodite cult site attracting worshippers from throughout the Mediterranean.

Archaeological evidence from the Acrocorinth confirms the sanctuary's existence — foundations of the temple, votive offerings, and associated structures have been identified. The temple was destroyed and rebuilt multiple times (Corinth was sacked by Rome in 146 BCE and refounded as a Roman colony in 44 BCE). In the Byzantine and Frankish periods the site became a Christian chapel and later a mosque. Today the Acrocorinth and its ancient sanctuary are preserved as an archaeological site accessible to visitors.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Temple of Aphrodite at Acrocorinth — whose alleged sacred prostitution made ancient Corinth proverbially synonymous with luxury and sensuality, whose scholarship continues to debate hierodouloi traditions, and which commanded the most strategically imposing position in the Peloponnese — is one of the ancient world's most historically discussed Aphrodite sanctuaries.
